items.stem: Explain the concept of balanced forces with the help of an example. What happens to the state of motion of an object when balanced forces act on it?
items.answer: Balanced forces occur when multiple forces acting on an object are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. Because the net force is zero, balanced forces do not change the state of rest or the state of uniform motion of the object. items.stem: Compare balanced and unbalanced forces with respect to their magnitude, direction, and their ultimate effect on the state of motion of an object.
items.answer: Balanced forces are two or more forces acting on an object that are exactly equal in magnitude but strictly opposite in direction. Because they cancel each other completely, their net force is zero, meaning they do not change the object’s state of rest or constant velocity. In contrast, unbalanced forces are unequal in magnitude or do not act in perfectly opposite directions. Once the acceleration is determined, you multiply it by the known mass of the car using Newton’s second law equation (F = ma) to calculate the exact net force acting upon it.

items.stem: When dealing with two attached objects like a cart towing a trailer, why do physicists often treat them as a single combined system? How does this mathematically simplify finding the acceleration?
items.answer: Physicists often treat connected objects as a single combined system to greatly simplify motion analysis. When viewed as one system, the complex internal forces acting between the individual objects—such as the tension in the towing rope— cancel each other out completely in pairs. This How Forces Affect Motion allows us to use Newton’s second law by simply dividing the total external pulling force by the combined total mass of both objects, effortlessly yielding the system’s overall acceleration without needing to solve multiple simultaneous equations.

items.stem: Have you ever noticed people cracking a fresh hard coconut in one go by hitting it forcefully on the ground? Explain the science behind how the shell breaks using Newton’s laws.
items.answer: Breaking a hard coconut in one go is a practical application of Newton’s second law of motion. When the fast-moving coconut violently hits the hard, unyielding ground, its velocity is abruptly reduced to absolute zero in a fraction of a second. Because the time duration of this impact is extremely short, the resulting deceleration is massively high. Consequently, the ground exerts an enormous reaction force back on the coconut shell, which surpasses its structural strength, causing it to instantly crack open.

items.stem: Imagine a hypothetical scenario where the force of friction completely disappears from the entire world. Describe two immediate severe consequences this would have on everyday human movement or transportation.
items.answer: If friction were to completely vanish from the world, the consequences would be catastrophic for daily activities. First, humans would be entirely unable to walk or run; without friction to provide a forward reaction force against our footsteps, we would simply slip uncontrollably in place. Second, wheeled vehicles like cars and bicycles could neither steer, accelerate, nor apply brakes safely. Any moving object on a flat path would simply glide forever at a constant speed, unable to deliberately stop or change direction. LON G Answer QUESTION

items.stem: (a) Draw a diagram showing the horizontal and vertical forces acting on a wooden block being pushed across a table but remaining completely stationary? (b) Identify the balanced force pairs? (c) Explain how Newton’s first law of motion applies to this specific situation?
items.answer: (a) (b) When a wooden block is pushed but remains stationary, multiple forces act upon it, but they form balanced pairs. The downward gravitational force exerted by the Earth is perfectly balanced by the upward normal force exerted by the table’s surface. Similarly, the applied horizontal push is completely balanced by an equal and opposite force of friction acting between the bottom of the block and the table. Since the opposing forces cancel each other out, the net force acting on the block is zero. (c) According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object at rest will remain at rest unless acted upon by a non-zero net force. Because the forces are balanced, the state of the block does not change, and it continues to remain completely stationary on the table without experiencing any acceleration.

items.stem: (a) What is the force of friction and what generally causes it? (b) Describe briefly how you would use a spring balance and a wooden block to show that friction depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact? (c) Why do we need to continuously apply a forward force to keep a bicycle moving at a constant velocity?
items.answer: (a) The force of friction is a resistive force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It arises due to the interactions and interlocking between the surfaces at the microscopic level. (b) To demonstrate that friction depends on the nature of the surfaces, place a wooden block on a normal table and pull it with a horizontally attached spring balance until it just starts moving. Note the reading, which indicates the force of friction. Repeat this experiment by placing the same block on different surfaces like polished marble or a laminated top. The varying spring balance readings will clearly indicate that rougher surfaces offer significantly greater friction than smoother ones. (c) Although Newton’s first law states objects move uniformly without external forces, we must continuously apply a pedal force to keep a bicycle moving to perfectly counter this ever-present friction and maintain a zero net force.

items.stem: (a) Draw a velocity-time graph showing the motion of a fast cricket ball being caught in two scenarios: an abrupt catch and a gradual catch where the fielder pulls their hands backwards? (b) Explain the scientific principle behind pulling the hands back using Newton’s second law? (c) How do vehicle airbags use this same principle during collisions?
items.answer: (a) (b) According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is inversely proportional to the time taken for a change in velocity. When a cricketer catches a fast-moving ball and pulls their hands backwards, they strategically increase the time duration over which the high velocity of the ball reduces to zero. This extended time significantly decreases the deceleration of the ball. Consequently, a much smaller net force is required to stop the ball, thereby minimising the impact and preventing serious injury to the fielder’s hands. (c) This identical scientific principle is applied in vehicle air-bags. During an abrupt collision, an air-bag inflates to provide a soft compressible cushion. It delays the passenger’s forward motion, increasing the time over which their velocity reaches zero. This critically reduces the acceleration and lowers the exerted force, substantially reducing the risk of fatal injuries.

items.stem: (a) State Newton’s second law of motion and express it mathematically? (b) A sports car of mass 1200 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to a velocity of 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the acceleration of the car and the net force acting on it?
items.answer: (a) Newton’s second law of motion states that when a net force acts on an object, it accelerates in the direction of the net force, where the magnitude of acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the object’s mass. Mathematically, it is expressed as a = F/m, which is commonly rearranged as F = ma, where F is the net force, m is the mass, and a is the acceleration. (b) For the sports car, the initial velocity is zero, and the final velocity is twenty metres per second over a time interval of four seconds. Using the kinematic equation, acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time, yielding five metres per second squared. Using the second law equation, the net force is the mass of twelve hundred kilograms multiplied by the acceleration of five, giving a net force of six thousand newtons.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 10 g travelling horizontally with a velocity of 150 ms–1 strikes a stationary wooden block and comes to rest in 0.03 s. Calculate the distance of penetration of the bullet into the block. Also calculate the magnitude of the force exerted by the wooden block on the bullet.
items.answer: (a) According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting upon it and inversely proportional to its mass. Therefore, if the applied net force is intentionally doubled while the mass is kept entirely constant, the resulting acceleration of the object will also be exactly doubled. (b) Conversely, if the mass of the object is doubled while applying the exact same constant force, the object inherently becomes heavier and much harder to move, causing the resulting acceleration to be strictly reduced to exactly half of its original value. (c) To calculate the urgently required force for the specific block, we apply the foundational mathematical equation Force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. By multiplying the block’s given mass of ten kilograms by the desired acceleration of two point five metres per second squared, we conclusively determine that a net force of twenty-five newtons is required.

items.stem: (a) Describe the general mechanism of a rocket launch into space using the principles of Newton’s third law of motion? (b) How did the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 use this exact same physical principle to intentionally slow down and achieve a successful soft landing near the Moon’s south pole?
items.answer: (a) A rocket launch is a classic and powerful demonstration of Newton’s third law of motion, which states that every action has an equal and opposite reaction acting on different bodies. During a launch, the rocket engine rapidly burns fuel to produce continuously expanding exhaust gases. The engine forcefully expels these highly pressurised gases downwards towards the ground. This deliberate downward push constitutes the action force. Simultaneously, the expelled exhaust gases exert an exactly equal and opposite reaction force upwards on the rocket itself. Because this upward thrust is significantly larger than the gravitational weight of the rocket, it smoothly accelerates upwards into space. (b) The Vikram lander ingeniously utilised this exact principle but in reverse for its lunar descent. By actively firing its thrusters in the downward direction of its motion, the expelled gases created a strong opposing upward reaction force. This counter-force deliberately reduced the lander’s velocity, enabling a completely safe soft landing. Numerical Question

items.stem: A stone of 1 kg is thrown with a velocity of 20 ms–1 across the frozen surface of a lake and comes to rest after travelling a distance of 50 m. What is the force of friction between the stone and the ice?
items.answer: Given, Mass m = 1 kg Initial velocity u = 20 ms–1 Final velocity v = 0 ms–1 Distance s = 50 m How Forces Affect Motion (b) This fundamental principle perfectly explains the mechanics of human walking. When you attempt to walk forward, your foot actively pushes against the ground in the backward direction. In immediate response, the ground applies an equal and opposite reaction force on your foot in the forward direction. It is this forward frictional force from the ground that actually propels your body ahead. (c) Although the action and reaction forces are completely equal in magnitude and strictly opposite in direction, they do not cancel each other out because they act on entirely different objects. One force forcefully acts on the ground while the opposite reaction force acts on your body, allowing net movement to successfully occur.

items.stem: (a) According to gravitational principles, the Earth and a falling apple exert equal and opposite forces on each other. Why does the apple fall towards the Earth, but the Earth does not visibly move towards the apple? (b) A 0.05 kg bullet is fired from a 4 kg gun with a force of 10 N; calculate the initial acceleration of both the bullet and the gun?
items.answer: (a) According to Newton’s third law, the Earth and a falling apple exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. However, Newton’s second law dictates that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. The mass of the Earth is astronomically larger compared to the tiny mass of the apple. Consequently, the same magnitude of force produces a significant, observable acceleration in the light apple, causing it to fall rapidly, but an infinitesimally small, unnoticeable acceleration in the massive Earth. (b) For the numerical portion, we use the formula acceleration equals force divided by mass. The initial acceleration of the bullet is calculated by dividing the ten newton force by its mass of zero point zero five kilograms, resulting in two hundred metres per second squared. The gun’s recoil acceleration is ten newtons divided by its four kilogram mass, yielding exactly two point five metres per second squared.

items.stem: (a) Draw the position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object moving along a straight line with a constant velocity? (b) Based on Newton’s first law, what is the net force acting on this object? (c) Explain why a moving object eventually comes to rest in the real world if no continuous forward push is applied?
items.answer: (a) (b) Based on Newton’s first law of motion, an object moving with a constant velocity has a strictly zero net force acting upon it. Because there is absolutely no change in either the speed or the direction of the object, its acceleration is zero, which mathematically confirms the complete absence of a net external force. In a theoretical frictionless environment, such an object would continue moving indefinitely. (c) However, in the real world, an object moving across a surface eventually comes to rest because forces are rarely completely absent. Even if no human pushes it, the unseen force of friction between the interacting surfaces, alongside air resistance, continuously acts in the direction directly opposite to the object’s motion. This unbalanced opposing force creates negative acceleration, gradually slowing the object down until it finally stops moving completely.

items.stem: A motorcar of mass 1200 kg is moving along a straight line with a uniform velocity of 90 km/h. Its velocity is slowed down to 18 km/h in 4 s by an unbalanced external force. Calculate the acceleration and change in momentum. Also calculate the magnitude of the force required.
items.answer: Mass of the motorcar, m = 1200 kg Initial velocity of the motorcar, u = 90 km/h = 25 m/s Final velocity of the motorcar, v = 18 km/h = 5 m/s Time taken, t = 4 s According to the first equation of motion : v = u + at 5 = 25 + a (4) a = – 5 m/s2 Negative sign indicates that its a retarding motion, i.e. velocity is decreasing. Change in momentum = mv – mu = m(v – u) = 1200 (5 – 25) = – 24000 kg ms–1 Force = Mass × Acceleration =1200 × – 5 = – 6000 N Acceleration of the motorcar = – 5 m/s2 Change in momentum of the motorcar = – 24000 kg ms–1 Hence, the force required to decrease the velocity is 6000 N. (Negative sign indicates retardation, decrease in momentum and retarding force)
